name: Kaya 0.1.43
changelog: A nicer read-out: after a Hint, the who-is-ahead bar is now a glossy capsule with a soft sheen and a clean divider at the split, instead of a flat black and white block. The hint marker still points the way in the accent colour.

history.1: First build: offline board, full rules and scoring, SGF, and a computer opponent.
history.2: Dark theme (Crake palette) with a light/dark toggle, plus a tidier header.
history.3: Crake electric-teal palette, stone-click sound, and a richer board.
history.5: Faster, stronger bot and a purpose-built tablet (landscape) layout.
history.6: Fail-safe update install (browser fallback) and a richer wood texture.
history.7: NFC tap-to-share (tap another phone to open Kaya's download page).
history.8: Stronger bot: RAVE search shares each playout across related moves for more purposeful, tougher play at the same speed.
history.9: Tighter bot: prunes pointless self-atari moves before searching, so it never slams a stone into nothing and reads deeper.
history.10: The computer ends decided games gracefully: when you pass and it is settled and ahead, it passes back instead of playing on.
history.11: A more handsome board: a proper goban frame with a heavier outer border and hairline inner lines, scaled to the board size.
history.12: A more tactical opponent: it now values captures, threats, and rescues by group size, so it goes after whole groups and defends its big ones.
history.13: The About screen now shows the real installed version, so every update is visible on the phone.
history.14: A far more tactical opponent: it now blocks when you atari it, and it puts your stones in atari and captures. Forcing moves no longer fade out of its reading.
history.15: Better shape: the bot now connects its own stones into strong groups and wedges to cut yours apart, so its stones work together.
history.16: The opponent now reads ladders: it favours ataris that actually run a stone down and capture, and no longer treats escaping ataris as wins.
history.17: A ko marker: when a recapture is forbidden by the ko rule, the board shows a small square on that point so it is clear why and where you cannot play yet.
history.18: A stronger read at the same speed: the bot's playouts are now forcing (they press weak groups into atari and follow up), so it judges fights far more accurately.
history.19: A clearer result: when the game is scored, each side shows where its points came from (territory + captures, or stones + area) with komi.
history.20: Easier to follow: the status line now names the move just played (e.g. "White played G5"), so you can find your opponent's stone at a glance.
history.21: Kaya remembers your setup: the New Game dialog opens on the size, ruleset, handicap, opponent, and difficulty you last played.
history.22: Resign now asks first (one tap arms it, the button becomes Confirm resign), so a stray tap can't end your game. New Game also truly remembers your last setup across launches.
history.23: Sensible openings: the computer now starts in the corners like real games, instead of dropping its first stones anywhere along the side.
history.24: No more hopeless ladders: the bot now reads whether a caught group can escape and stops running one that is lost, instead of feeding you more stones.
history.25: A tougher default: the Medium computer (where every new game starts) now reads deeper and plays stronger, while still moving in about a second.
history.26: Better opening shape: in the opening the computer no longer attaches onto your lone stones, it approaches from a distance and takes big points instead.
history.27: Games feel fresh: the computer now varies its play from game to game instead of opening the same corner and answering identically every time.
history.28: Complete saved games: SGF exports now record the ruleset and the result on a resignation, so they open with the right rules and winner in other Go software.
history.29: Sharper fighting: the computer now spots a double atari (one move forking two of your groups) and no longer over-values touching a single group from several sides.
history.30: A smarter Easy opponent: it now saves its own groups when you atari them instead of letting them die, and varies its play from game to game.
history.31: Defends earlier: the computer reinforces a group that is down to two liberties and under attack, before you can push it into atari.
history.32: Opens more game files: SGFs with variations (game reviews, problem sets) now load along the main line instead of muddling every branch together.
history.33: Complete results in saved games: a game that ends by counting now records its final score in the SGF (e.g. B+12.5), not just resignations.
history.34: Graceful concessions: when the computer is hopelessly behind in a developed game it resigns instead of making you capture everything, but never early off a shaky read.
history.35: Share your games: on Android, Save SGF now opens the share sheet to send a finished game (with ruleset and result) to Files, Drive, email, or a chat.
history.36: A slightly sharper read: the computer no longer wastes exploration on pointless first-line moves, so its sense of who is ahead is cleaner and its play a touch stronger.
history.37: A more beautiful board: the wood now catches a soft warm light toward the centre and settles into richer edges, like a real lit goban. Lovely in the dark theme.
history.38: Glossier stones: each stone now catches a small point of light, so black slate and white shell look polished and three-dimensional against the lit board.
history.39: A more refined New Game dialog: settings sit under small-cap section headers with more breathing room, and a soft divider sets your choices apart from Start game. Tidy in both themes.
history.40: A polished Kaya mark: the two stones in the logo (and the little header mark) now catch the same shading and glossy light as the stones on the board, and the About logo lifts off the panel with a soft shadow.
history.41: Nicer player cards: the little Black and White stones on the two player pills are now real, shaded stones with a soft shadow, matching the board and logo. The White marker no longer fades into the cream panel.
history.42: A board with real depth: the wood now has a beveled edge, catching light along the top and left and settling into shadow at the bottom and right, so it reads as a solid slab of kaya on the table. Especially lovely in the dark theme.
history.43: Tidier scoring: when the game is counted, the territory marks are now smaller, softly rounded, and gently outlined, so they read as delicate points on the wood instead of heavy blocks. The white marks no longer melt into the board.
history.44: A nicer read-out: after a Hint, the who-is-ahead bar is now a glossy capsule with a soft sheen and a clean divider at the split, instead of a flat black and white block. The hint marker still points the way in the accent colour.
